topic.angle: High-yield crops and the people who fed more of the world

panels.text: The Rockefeller Foundation funded an agricultural station in Mexico to breed corn and wheat for dry climates. It hired a young agronomist named Norman Borlaug.
The Green Revolution that followed spread high-yielding crops, especially dwarf wheat and rice. The new seeds needed far more fertiliser, plus pesticides and controlled irrigation.
In Asia, a rice called IR8 yielded about 10 times as much as traditional rice under the best conditions. It was nicknamed 'Miracle Rice'.

India's rice yields were about two tons per hectare in the 1960s and about six by the mid-1990s. Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize and is credited with saving over a billion people from starvation.
